stated.text: The service is written in Node.js, with server.js as the server.
The service uses no npm dependencies.
server.js listens on the port given in the PORT environment variable.
The service keeps its data in the JSON file named by the DATA_FILE environment variable.
Groups survive a restart of the server with the same DATA_FILE.
Expenses survive a restart of the server with the same DATA_FILE.
POST /groups with {"id": "<group id>", "members": ["<name>", ...]} creates a group and answers 201.
POST /groups answers 409 if a group with that id already exists.
POST /groups answers 400 when members holds fewer than two names.
POST /groups answers 400 when members holds fewer than two distinct names (for example ["Ann", "Ann"]).
POST /groups answers 400 when members holds fewer than two non-empty names (for example ["Ann", ""]).
POST /groups/<id>/expenses records an expense paid by one member, the payer.
An expense {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "equal"} is shared equally among all members of the group.
For split "equal", any cents left over after an even division go one each to the members listed first in the group's members order.
An expense {"payer": "<name>", "cents": <positive integer>, "split": "exact", "shares": {"<name>": <cents>, ...}} makes each member listed in shares owe that many whole cents.
For split "exact", a share of zero is allowed.
For split "exact", the shares must add up to cents.
A recorded expense answers 201 with {"expense": <n>}.
The expense number n is 1 for the group's first expense, then 2, and so on.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown payer.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown member (a name in shares that is not a group member).
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for a non-positive amount.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for a non-integer amount.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for an unknown split.
POST /groups/<id>/expenses answers 400 for shares that do not add up to cents.
GET /groups/<id>/balances returns an object with each member's net cents.
A member's net cents are what they paid minus what they owe.
The balances returned by GET /groups/<id>/balances add up to 0.
GET /groups/<id>/settlements returns a JSON array of {"from", "to", "cents"} payments.
The settlement payments bring every balance to 0.
Settlements are built by repeatedly having the member who owes most pay the member who is owed most the smaller of the two amounts.
In settlements, ties (between debtors or between creditors) go to the member listed first.
Every route under /groups/<id> answers 404 for an unknown group.
Concurrent requests never lose an expense.
The behaviour is covered by node:test tests under test/ that run with `node --test`.

unstated.text: What status a request body that is not valid JSON gets, and whether the server keeps serving afterwards.
unstated.why: Client code and the operator need a predictable refusal for a truncated or garbled body; a 500 or a crashed process would take down every group's service.
unstated.probe: Start the server. POST /groups with Content-Type application/json and the raw body `{` (and separately `not json`). Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"] and POST /groups/g/expenses with the raw body `not json`. Record each status and body. Then POST a valid new group and GET /groups/g/balances and check both still work.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for each broken body, with or without an error message, is the fitting answer; another 4xx is acceptable. The server must stay up and answer the following valid requests; nothing is stored from the broken body.

unstated.text: What happens when a required field is missing: an expense without payer, cents or split, split "exact" without shares, or a group without id or members.
unstated.why: These are the first bad requests a client sends; the stated 400 list does not name a missing field, and a throw becomes a 500 or a dead process instead of a refusal.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"]. POST /groups/g/expenses with {}, with {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100}, with {"cents": 100, "split": "equal"}, with {"payer": "Ann", "split": "equal"}, and with {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "exact"}. POST /groups with {} and with {"id": "h"}. Record each status and body, then GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for each, with no expense or group stored, and the server still answering. A 500 is a worse fit; a crash is not acceptable.

unstated.text: Whether JSON values of the wrong type are refused or coerced: cents as a string, members as a string, a member that is not a string, or shares that is not an object.
unstated.why: A client sending "100" instead of 100 looks like the documented call; the request's 400 list names only non-integer amounts, so the service may coerce, refuse, or crash.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": "Ann,Bob"} and {"id": "g1", "members": ["Ann", 7, "Bob"]}. Create group g2 with ["Ann","Bob"]. POST /groups/g2/expenses with {"payer": "Ann", "cents": "100", "split": "equal"}, with {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": [100]}. Record each status; for any 201 GET /groups/g2/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for each is fine. Coercing the string "100" to 100 and answering 201 is also fine if consistent. No 500 or crash; splitting the string "Ann,Bob" into members is not required.

unstated.text: Which group ids are accepted (empty, missing, numeric, containing '/', spaces, '%', unicode), and whether every group that got 201 can then be addressed through /groups/<id>/ by all three group routes, percent-encoded where the path needs it.
unstated.why: The id is the only way to address a group later; a group created with an id that no later request can reach is lost to the customer.
unstated.probe: Separately POST /groups with valid members and ids "", none, 1, "a/b", "a b", "50%" and "café". For each 201, GET balances and settlements and POST a valid expense at the path formed from the id, percent-encoded where needed (for example /groups/a%20b/balances, /groups/a%2Fb/balances). Record statuses.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for empty, missing or non-string ids is fine. Rejecting awkward or overlong ids with 400, or accepting them, are both fine, as long as every id that got 201 is reachable by balances, settlements and expenses.

unstated.text: Whether exact shares may be negative or non-integer (for example {"Ann": 150, "Bob": -50} or {"Ann": 50.5, "Bob": 49.5} for cents 100), since only zero is said to be allowed and only the total is said to be checked.
unstated.why: A negative share credits a member who paid nothing and moves debt the wrong way; fractional shares break the whole-cent balances and settlements.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"]. POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"Ann": 150, "Bob": -50}}, then {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"Ann": 50.5, "Bob": 49.5}}. Record both statuses and GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 for fractional shares is the fitting reading of 'whole cents'. 400 for negative shares is the expected reading; accepting integer negative shares is a judgement call only if documented. Balances stay whole cents summing to 0.

unstated.text: How a member list is handled when it holds two distinct non-empty names plus a duplicate, an empty or whitespace-only entry (for example ["Ann", "Ann", "Bob"] or ["Ann", " ", "Bob"]), and whether names differing only in case or surrounding spaces count as distinct.
unstated.why: A duplicated member counted twice changes an equal split and who gets the leftover cents; customers typing names by hand will hit these cases.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "d", "members": ["Ann", "Ann", "Bob"]}; if 201, POST /groups/d/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "equal"} and GET /groups/d/balances. POST /groups {"id": "w", "members": ["Ann", " ", "Bob"]}, {"id": "s", "members": [" ", "Bob"]} and {"id": "c", "members": ["Ann", "ann"]}. Record statuses and any balances.
unstated.fine_answers: Rejecting a list with a repeated name with 400, or accepting it and de-duplicating while keeping first-listed order, are both fine; a member must never be counted twice. Case variants being distinct is fine; whitespace-only names rejected or accepted are both defensible if consistent.

unstated.text: Whether an exact split must list every member, or a member left out of shares owes nothing.
unstated.why: Users splitting a bill among part of the group need omitted members to be uncharged or a clear refusal.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob","Cho"]. POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "exact", "shares": {"Ann": 40, "Bob": 60}}; record the status and, for 201, GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 201 with Cho at 0, Ann +60 and Bob -60 is the plain reading of 'each member listed in shares'. 400 because a member is absent is defensible if documented. Charging Cho anything is not acceptable.

unstated.text: Whether an expense or group is already safely written to DATA_FILE when its 201 is sent, and whether a crash or kill during a write can leave DATA_FILE truncated or corrupt.
unstated.why: The customer was promised that data survives a restart and no expense is lost; an operator restarting after a crash must not find an unreadable file and lose every group.
unstated.probe: Start with DATA_FILE set to a new path, create group g, POST an expense and send SIGKILL to the server as soon as the 201 arrives. Restart with the same DATA_FILE and GET /groups/g/balances; check the file parses as JSON. Repeat while sending many POSTs in a loop and killing mid-stream; check the file still parses and every expense that got 201 is reflected.
unstated.fine_answers: Every acknowledged write is present after restart and the file always parses (for example a write to a temporary file then rename before replying). A synchronous write before replying without atomic rename is weaker but acceptable at this scale.

unstated.text: What the server does when DATA_FILE names a file that does not exist yet.
unstated.why: An operator's first start is on an empty machine; the request says data lives in that file, not that it already exists.
unstated.probe: Run server.js with PORT set and DATA_FILE set to an absent file in an existing directory. Check whether it starts, whether the file appears at startup or on the first write, then POST a valid group, stop, read the file, restart and GET the group's balances.
unstated.fine_answers: Starting with an empty store, creating the file at startup or on the first successful write, and finding the group after restart. Failing at start is not acceptable for an absent file in a writable directory.

unstated.text: What the server does at startup when DATA_FILE is empty or holds invalid JSON.
unstated.why: A corrupt or hand-edited file must not be silently replaced with an empty store, which would wipe the customer's data.
unstated.probe: Write `{broken` into the DATA_FILE and start the server; record whether it refuses to start, starts empty, or starts and later overwrites the file. Repeat with an empty file; if it starts, create a group and check whether the original file content was preserved.
unstated.fine_answers: Refusing to start with a clear error, or starting while preserving the bad file (for example renamed aside), are fine. Silently overwriting it is not.

unstated.text: What server.js does when DATA_FILE is unset.
unstated.why: An operator who forgets the variable should get a clear failure or a documented default, not data written to an unexpected place.
unstated.probe: Run node server.js with PORT set and DATA_FILE unset. Record whether it exits with a message or keeps running; if it runs, POST a valid group and find where, if anywhere, data was written.
unstated.fine_answers: Exiting with a clear error, or using a documented default path, are both fine.

unstated.text: What server.js does when PORT is unset, empty, not a port number, or 0.
unstated.why: The person starting the process has only 'listens on PORT'; a missing or bad value is the usual first mistake and they need to know whether it exits, picks a default, or binds an ephemeral port.
unstated.probe: Run node server.js with DATA_FILE set and PORT unset; then PORT=abc; then PORT=0. Each time record the exit status, any message, and, if it stays up, which port accepts a connection.
unstated.fine_answers: Exiting non-zero with a message for a missing or invalid port, or listening on a documented default, are fine. For PORT=0, exiting, or listening on an ephemeral port, are both fine.

unstated.text: Whether concurrent expense posts to one group each get a distinct expense number with no repeats or gaps, and each acknowledged expense is applied exactly once.
unstated.why: Expense numbers are how users refer to expenses; two expenses both numbered 3, or one applied twice, means the ledger is wrong.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"]. Fire 100 POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 2, "split": "equal"} at once. Collect every status and expense number, then GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: The numbers on the 201s are exactly 1..N, each once, in any order across responses; Ann's net is N and Bob's -N. Some requests failing is fine if each 201 is reflected once and failures leave nothing stored.

unstated.text: Whether a balances read that overlaps in-flight expense posts returns a consistent state.
unstated.why: A balances view that does not sum to 0, cannot be shown to users checking who owes what.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"]. Send 20 POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "equal"} without waiting, and while they are in flight GET /groups/g/balances several times and sum each body. Then GET balances once after all POSTs finish.
unstated.fine_answers: Every read sums to 0 and reflects a whole number of expenses; a read during the burst may omit an unfinished POST.

unstated.text: What two overlapping POST /groups calls for the same new id do.
unstated.why: Two people can create the same group at once; two 201s, a group stored twice, or a last-write-wins member list breaks the 409 rule under the only load the request mentions.
unstated.probe: With an empty DATA_FILE, send 20 concurrent POST /groups {"id": "race", "members": ["Ann","Bob"]} (or two with different member lists). Count 201s and 409s, GET /groups/race/balances, restart with the same DATA_FILE and GET again.
unstated.fine_answers: Exactly one 201 and the rest 409, one stored group whose members are those of the 201 request, the same after restart.

unstated.text: Whether expense numbering continues after a restart instead of starting again at 1.
unstated.why: Users refer to expenses by number; restarting the numbers would give two expenses the same number in one group.
unstated.probe: Create group g, POST three expenses, restart with the same DATA_FILE, POST one more expense and record the number.
unstated.fine_answers: The next expense is numbered 4.

unstated.text: How unknown paths and wrong methods are answered (GET /groups, DELETE /groups/g, POST /groups/g/balances, GET /groups/g/unknown, GET /other).
unstated.why: Client developers need to tell a typo from a missing group; the request only says unknown groups get 404.
unstated.probe: Create group g. Send GET /groups, DELETE /groups/g, POST /groups/g/balances, GET /groups/g/expenses, GET /groups/g/unknown, GET /other and GET /groups/g/balances/extra. Record statuses and check the server still answers afterwards.
unstated.fine_answers: 404 or 405 for an unknown path or wrong method are both fine. The server must not hang, crash, or treat them as a valid route.

unstated.text: What Content-Type the responses carry.
unstated.why: Clients and tools decide how to parse a response from its Content-Type; JSON sent as text/html or with no type trips them.
unstated.probe: Create group g, POST an expense, GET /groups/g/balances and /groups/g/settlements, and trigger a 400 and a 404. Record the Content-Type header of each response.
unstated.fine_answers: application/json (optionally with charset) on JSON bodies is expected; an error with no body may carry no Content-Type.

unstated.text: What body, if any, POST /groups returns with its 201, and whether a Location header is set.
unstated.why: A client or a test has to know whether to parse JSON, read an empty body, or follow a Location header after creating a group.
unstated.probe: Start the server. POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": ["Ann","Bob"]}. Record the status, headers and raw body.
unstated.fine_answers: An empty body, plain text, or a JSON object (for example echoing id and members) are all fine; a Location header may be present or absent.

unstated.text: What body a 400, 409 or 404 carries.
unstated.why: Whoever calls the API, or debugs a failure, cannot tell a refusal's reason from a bare status, and a client may try to parse the body as JSON.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": ["Ann"]}. POST a valid group g, then the same body again. GET /groups/missing/balances. POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 0, "split": "equal"}. Record each status and raw body.
unstated.fine_answers: An empty body, a plain-text reason, or a JSON error object are all fine; the statuses need not share one shape.

unstated.text: Which status POST /groups uses when the id already exists and the member list is also invalid, and whether the stored members change.
unstated.why: A retry that reuses an id with a bad body is a normal client mistake; the caller must know which case it hit, and the original members must not be replaced.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": ["Ann","Bob"]}. POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": ["Ann"]}. Record the status, then GET /groups/g/balances and check which names are keys.
unstated.fine_answers: 400 or 409 are both fine; the stored members stay Ann and Bob.

unstated.text: Which status is used when the group is unknown and the expense body is also invalid.
unstated.why: The request states 404 for an unknown group and 400 for a bad expense separately; a client branching on status needs to know which check wins.
unstated.probe: Without creating it, POST /groups/no-such/expenses with {} and with {"payer": "Ann", "cents": -5, "split": "equal"}. Record both statuses.
unstated.fine_answers: 404 or 400 are both fine for each; nothing is created.

unstated.text: Whether extra fields on an otherwise valid body are ignored, stored or rejected, including a shares object sent with split "equal".
unstated.why: Clients add notes and titles; a strict server fails those calls, and a server that applies shares on an equal split changes who owes what.
unstated.probe: POST /groups {"id": "g", "members": ["Ann","Bob"], "title": "Trip"}. If 201, POST /groups/g/expenses {"payer": "Ann", "cents": 100, "split": "equal", "note": "dinner", "shares": {"Ann": 10, "Bob": 10}}. Record statuses and GET /groups/g/balances.
unstated.fine_answers: 201 ignoring or storing extra fields, or 400 for an unexpected field, are fine. If the equal split is accepted, Ann is +50 and Bob -50; rejecting it because the shares do not add up is also fine.

unstated.text: Whether a JSON body must be sent with Content-Type: application/json.
unstated.why: A client or curl command that omits the header or sends text/plain is either accepted or refused, and the request does not say which.
unstated.probe: POST /groups a valid body with no Content-Type header, and another valid body (different id) with Content-Type: text/plain. Record both statuses.
unstated.fine_answers: 201 for both is fine; 400 or 415 unless the header is application/json is also fine.

unstated.text: Whether GET /groups/<id>/balances and GET /groups/<id>/settlements only read, or also change stored state.
unstated.why: A client that polls the settlement plan would wipe the debts if the GET recorded the payments.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"], POST an equal expense paid by Ann for 100. GET balances, GET settlements, GET balances, GET settlements, and compare the bodies.
unstated.fine_answers: Both balances bodies match and both settlements bodies match; the GETs write nothing.

unstated.text: Whether DATA_FILE written by the server is read back to the same state: a group with both an equal and an exact expense gives the same balances, settlements and next expense number after restart.
unstated.why: The next maintainer has to inspect or repair the only copy of the data, and a file the server cannot read back as written loses the customer's ledger.
unstated.probe: Point DATA_FILE at a new path. Create a group, record one equal and one exact expense, and copy the balances and settlements bodies. Read DATA_FILE while the server is up. Restart with the same file, GET balances and settlements, compare, and POST one more expense.
unstated.fine_answers: Any JSON layout the server writes and reads back with identical balances and settlements and the next number 3 is fine; balances may be stored or computed on read. A hand-written file of another shape does not have to load.

unstated.text: Whether the tests are self-contained: they start their own server on a free port with a temporary DATA_FILE, need nothing running, leave no stray files or processes, and pass repeatedly.
unstated.why: The next maintainer runs `node --test` on a fresh checkout or in CI; tests needing a fixed port or a real data file fail or clobber data.
unstated.probe: On a clean checkout with nothing listening, run `node --test` from the project root twice in a row, and once while another process holds a common port such as 3000. Check the exit code is 0 each time, no new files remain in the project folder, and no node process is left running.
unstated.fine_answers: Any self-contained approach (spawning server.js on port 0 or a free port, or importing the server) is fine.

unstated.text: When a write to DATA_FILE fails (unwritable file or directory, full disk), a refused expense or group creation leaves no trace: reads do not show it, it is absent after restart, the expense numbering is unchanged and a refused group id stays free.
unstated.why: A caller told 'failed' will retry; if the failed write still shows up later the expense is counted twice, and if a refused group id is taken the customer cannot create it.
unstated.probe: Create group g and record expense 1. Make DATA_FILE (or its directory) unwritable without changing its contents. POST a valid expense to g and a valid new group h; record statuses and GET /groups/g/balances and /groups/h/balances. Restore write access, restart with the same DATA_FILE, GET both again, then POST an expense to g and POST group h with a different member list.
unstated.fine_answers: The failed requests get a 5xx (any explicit failure status) and the server stays up. Balances show expense 1 alone before and after restart, h is 404, the next expense to g returns {"expense": 2}, and creating h then returns 201 with the new members. Answering 201 for a write that did not persist is not acceptable.

unstated.text: How amounts and running totals beyond JavaScript's safe integer range (about 9.007e15 cents) are handled.
unstated.why: A large or accumulated amount that loses precision silently gives wrong balances and settlements that no longer add up to 0.
unstated.probe: Create group g with ["Ann","Bob"]. POST an expense with cents 9007199254740993 (above the safe range), then several expenses of 9007199254740991 each. Record statuses and GET balances and settlements, checking exact sums.
unstated.fine_answers: Refusing amounts or totals beyond a documented limit with 400, or handling them exactly (for example with BigInt), are both fine. Accepting them and returning balances that are rounded or do not sum to 0 is not.

unstated.text: Whether very large request bodies are limited.
unstated.why: Without a limit, one oversized request can exhaust the server's memory and take every group offline.
unstated.probe: POST /groups and POST /groups/<id>/expenses with a 100 MB body (for example a huge members array or padding), then send a normal request. Record the status, the server's memory use and whether it still answers.
unstated.fine_answers: Refusing oversized bodies with 413 or 400 and staying up is the fitting answer; accepting a large body while staying responsive is also acceptable. Crashing or hanging is not.

unstated.text: Whether a group creation and an expense in another group, sent at the same time, both survive a restart.
unstated.why: Two writes that each rewrite the whole data file can drop each other; the request promises concurrent requests never lose an expense and that groups survive restarts.
unstated.probe: With an existing group g, send at the same time POST /groups {"id": "h", "members": ["Cy","Di"]} and POST /groups/g/expenses with a valid expense. After both return 201, restart with the same DATA_FILE and GET /groups/g/balances and /groups/h/balances. Repeat many times.
unstated.fine_answers: Every time, g's balances include the expense and h exists with members Cy and Di.

unstated.text: Whether member names that coincide with JavaScript object properties ("__proto__", "constructor", "toString") work throughout the API.
unstated.why: A member called "constructor" or "__proto__" can be mistaken for a built-in property, giving wrong balances, missing keys, or a crash.
unstated.probe: Create a group with ["__proto__","constructor","toString"]. POST an exact expense of 1 cent paid by toString with shares {"__proto__": 1}. GET balances and settlements.
unstated.fine_answers: Either refusing such names with 400 at creation, or, if accepted, balances with all three names as keys at -1, 0 and 1, and one 1-cent settlement from __proto__ to toString. A crash or a missing key is not acceptable.

unstated.text: Whether whole-cent values written in an equivalent JSON number form (1.0, 10e-1, 1e2) are accepted as integers.
unstated.why: JSON libraries in other languages write whole numbers as 100.0 or 1e2; refusing them, or treating them as different amounts, breaks those clients.
unstated.probe: In a group with Ana and Bo, send a raw exact expense body with Ana paying, cents written as 10e-1 and shares {"Ana":0.0,"Bo":1.0}; then the same with cents 1 and shares {"Ana":0,"Bo":1} in a second group. Compare statuses and balances.
unstated.fine_answers: Accepting both with identical balances, or consistently refusing the non-canonical spelling with 400, are both fine; accepting it but storing a different amount is not.

unstated.text: Whether every group in DATA_FILE stays reachable after a restart, including one whose id would be refused for a new group.
unstated.why: A limit on new ids added later, or a stored id the service would now refuse, must not cut the customer off from a group they already have.
unstated.probe: Create groups with the longest and most unusual ids the build accepts (and, where a later build adds a tighter id limit, start it on the earlier DATA_FILE). Restart, GET balances and settlements and POST an expense for each group, then restart again and GET balances.
unstated.fine_answers: Every stored group remains reachable under its original id, with its members, balances and next expense number preserved, across restarts.

unstated.text: What happens when a client disconnects in the middle of sending a request body.
unstated.why: A dropped mobile connection is ordinary; an unhandled request error can crash the process or store a half-read expense.
unstated.probe: Create group g. Open a connection, send POST /groups/g/expenses headers with Content-Length 1000 and only part of a body, then close the socket. Repeat several times, then GET /groups/g/balances and POST a valid expense.
unstated.fine_answers: No expense is stored from the aborted requests, the server stays up, and the following requests work.

unstated.text: Which Node.js versions the service needs, and whether it works on the versions an operator is likely to have.
unstated.why: A server that silently relies on a very recent Node feature fails at the first balances request on an operator's older but supported Node.
unstated.probe: Run server.js and `node --test` on the current and the previous active LTS releases of Node. Create a group, POST an expense, GET balances and settlements on each, and check for any stated minimum version.
unstated.fine_answers: Working on the active LTS releases, or stating a minimum version and failing at start with a clear message below it, are fine. Starting and then failing only on some requests is not.
